mainEntity.name: What is the standard order of a board meeting agenda?

acceptedAnswer.text: Call to order, roll call and quorum, approval of the agenda, approval of prior minutes, consent agenda, reports, old business, new business, executive session if needed, announcements and adjournment. Bylaws can change this order. Many boards also move key decisions earlier, so directors discuss them while they are fresh.

mainEntity.name: Who sets the board meeting agenda?

acceptedAnswer.text: The board chair sets the agenda, usually with the CEO or executive director and the board secretary. Directors can request items through the chair. Committee chairs submit their reports in advance, and the final version goes out with the packet so every director sees one identical plan.

mainEntity.name: How far in advance should a board agenda be sent?

acceptedAnswer.text: Send the agenda and packet 5 to 7 days ahead so directors can read the reports. State law sets only the floor for notice, not the packet: a California nonprofit calling a special meeting owes its directors 4 days by first-class mail, or 48 hours by phone, personal delivery or electronic transmission.

mainEntity.name: Is an agenda required for a board meeting?

acceptedAnswer.text: Notice is often required; an agenda often is not. California nonprofits are a clear case: Corporations Code section 7211 says a notice or waiver "need not specify the purpose" of any regular or special board meeting. Your bylaws may demand more than the statute, so read them before relying on this.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between old business and new business?

acceptedAnswer.text: Old business covers items carried over; new business covers matters raised for the first time. One trap: moving to "table" an item does not park it until next month. Robert's Rules says Lay on the Table only sets a question aside temporarily, and Postpone to a Certain Time is the motion that moves it to a later meeting.

The board meets privately, often without staff, on CEO performance, legal matters or personnel. Minutes usually record only that the session happened and its general topic.
